claim: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) uniquely require binding of two different neurotransmitter agonists for synaptic transmission.
source: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) uniquely require binding of two different neurotransmitter agonists for synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of NMDARs supported by the citation Hansen et al., 2021 in the introduction.

claim: D-serine and glycine bind to the GluN1 subunit of NMDARs.
source: D-serine and glycine bind to one subunit, GluN1, while glutamate binds to the other, GluN2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Glutamate binds to the GluN2 subunit of NMDARs.
source: D-serine and glycine bind to one subunit, GluN1, while glutamate binds to the other, GluN2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: D-serine binds to both GluN1 and GluN2A ligand-binding domains in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Surprisingly, we observed D-serine binding to both GluN1 and GluN2A LBDs, suggesting that D-serine competes with glutamate for binding to GluN2A.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multi-microsecond molecular dynamics simulations performed in this study.

claim: D-serine competes with glutamate for binding to GluN2A.
source: Surprisingly, we observed D-serine binding to both GluN1 and GluN2A LBDs, suggesting that D-serine competes with glutamate for binding to GluN2A.
evidence: This is inferred from simulation observations and confirmed by electrophysiology experiments.

claim: D-serine is inhibitory at high concentrations.
source: This mechanism is confirmed by our electrophysiology experiments, which show that D-serine is indeed inhibitory at high concentrations.
evidence: This is confirmed by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: D-serine stabilizes the closed GluN2A LBD conformation according to free energy calculations.
source: Although free energy calculations indicate that D-serine stabilizes the closed GluN2A LBD, its inhibitory behavior suggests that it either does not remain bound long enough or does not generate sufficient force for ion channel gating.
evidence: This is based on umbrella sampling free energy calculations shown in Figure 3.

claim: D-serine either does not remain bound long enough or does not generate sufficient force for ion channel gating despite stabilizing the closed GluN2A LBD.
source: Although free energy calculations indicate that D-serine stabilizes the closed GluN2A LBD, its inhibitory behavior suggests that it either does not remain bound long enough or does not generate sufficient force for ion channel gating.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the combined simulation and electrophysiology data.

claim: N-linked glycans primarily regulate NMDAR LBD binding by stabilizing the closed LBD through interactions with the LBD bottom lobe.
source: These conformation-dependent pathways were not significantly impacted by the presence of N-linked glycans, which act primarily by interacting with the LBD bottom lobe to stabilize the closed LBD.
evidence: This is based on analysis of glycosylated vs non-glycosylated simulations and glycan PMF calculations shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The NMDAR is a heterotetrameric ion channel comprising at least two different subunits, GluN1 and GluN2, assembled as a dimer of GluN1/GluN2 heterodimers.
source: This heterotetrameric ion channel comprises at least two different subunits, GluN1 (isoforms 1–4 a and 1-4b) and GluN2 (subtypes A-D), assembled as a dimer of GluN1/GluN2 heterodimers (Karakas and Furukawa, 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Glycine had been traditionally considered the major GluN1 agonist.
source: Traditionally, glycine had been considered the major GluN1 agonist (Johnson and Ascher, 1987; Forsythe et al., 1988; Kleckner and Dingledine, 1988), but more recent work has suggested that D-serine may in fact be the dominant co-agonist for synaptic NMDARs in the brain (Papouin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by historical citations.

claim: D-serine may be the dominant co-agonist for synaptic NMDARs in the brain.
source: Traditionally, glycine had been considered the major GluN1 agonist (Johnson and Ascher, 1987; Forsythe et al., 1988; Kleckner and Dingledine, 1988), but more recent work has suggested that D-serine may in fact be the dominant co-agonist for synaptic NMDARs in the brain (Papouin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Papouin et al., 2012.

claim: D-serine is synthesized by the enzyme serine racemase expressed in astroglia and neurons.
source: D-serine is synthesized by the enzyme serine racemase expressed in astroglia (Wolosker et al., 1999) and neurons (Miya et al., 2008; Balu et al., 2014) and is released into the postsynapse by the Asc-1 transporter (Rutter et al., 2007; Coyle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: D-serine is released into the postsynapse by the Asc-1 transporter.
source: D-serine is synthesized by the enzyme serine racemase expressed in astroglia (Wolosker et al., 1999) and neurons (Miya et al., 2008; Balu et al., 2014) and is released into the postsynapse by the Asc-1 transporter (Rutter et al., 2007; Coyle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: D-serine binding to synaptic NMDARs is responsible for inducing long-term potentiation (LTP), which is critical for memory functions.
source: D-serine binding to these synaptic NMDARs is responsible for inducing long-term potentiation (LTP), which is critical for memory functions (Henneberger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Henneberger et al., 2010.

claim: D-serine could be a promising therapeutic for the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders including schizophrenia and PTSD.
source: In addition, recent clinical efforts have indicated that D-serine could be a promising therapeutic for the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders (Peyrovian et al., 2019; MacKay et al., 2019), most notably schizophrenia (Kantrowitz et al., 2010) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Heresco-Levy et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple clinical study citations.

claim: NMDAR ligand-binding domains adopt a bi-lobed clamshell architecture that closes upon agonist binding.
source: The LBDs adopt a bi-lobed clamshell architecture that closes upon agonist binding (Yao et al., 2013; Jespersen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and computational studies.

claim: Conformational transitions of the LBDs from open to closed clamshells result in the generation of tension in the LBD-TMD linkers, which facilitates gating of the TMD channel.
source: The conformational transitions of the LBDs from open to closed clamshells result in the generation of tension in the LBD-TMD linkers, which in turn facilitates gating of the TMD channel (Tajima et al., 2016; Chou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Glycine binding to the GluN1 LBD and glutamate binding to the GluN2A LBD drives the conformational equilibrium toward the closed LBD.
source: Previous computational studies of NMDAR LBDs have indicated that glycine binding to the GluN1 LBD and glutamate binding to the GluN2A LBD drives the conformational equilibrium toward the closed LBD (Yao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous computational work.

claim: The binding pose of D-serine in the closed GluN1 LBD has been determined by crystallographic studies.
source: While crystallographic studies have determined the binding pose of D-serine in the closed GluN1 LBD (Furukawa and Gouaux, 2003), the molecular mechanisms by which D-serine finds its way into and stabilizes NMDAR LBDs are not well understood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a crystal structure.

claim: Glycine binds to the GluN1 subunit by freely diffusing into the binding pocket through an 'unguided' diffusion mechanism.
source: Specifically, they found that glycine binds to the GluN1 subunit by freely diffusing into the binding pocket, where it is trapped by energetically favorable interactions with key binding site residues.
evidence: This is based on previous simulation studies cited in the text.

claim: Glutamate binds to GluN2A through a 'guided' diffusion mechanism where it contacts residues along the protein surface that help guide it into the binding pocket.
source: Glutamate, on the other hand, was found to contact residues along the protein surface that helped guide itself into its binding pocket, positioning it to interact stably with residues in the binding site.
evidence: This is based on previous simulation studies cited in the text.

claim: 99 guided-diffusion pathways for D-serine binding to GluN2A were identified in approximately 51 μs of simulation.
source: In our aggregate ~51 μs of sampling of the glycosylated GluN1/GluN2A LBD dimer, we identified 99 guided-diffusion pathways for GluN2A and 104 (plus 23 free diffusion events) for GluN1.
evidence: This is a direct result from the simulation data analysis.

claim: 104 guided-diffusion pathways plus 23 free diffusion events for D-serine binding to GluN1 were identified in approximately 51 μs of simulation.
source: In our aggregate ~51 μs of sampling of the glycosylated GluN1/GluN2A LBD dimer, we identified 99 guided-diffusion pathways for GluN2A and 104 (plus 23 free diffusion events) for GluN1.
evidence: This is a direct result from the simulation data analysis.

claim: Pathway similarity analysis can be used to quantify the spatial and geometric similarity between pairs of ligand binding paths.
source: To address this, we applied pathway similarity analysis (PSA) (Seyler et al., 2015) to quantify the spatial and geometric similarity between pairs of paths (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a methodological approach applied in this study, with citation to the original method.

claim: Four distinct spatial clusters of D-serine binding pathways to GluN2A were identified through cluster analysis.
source: For GluN2A, cluster analysis revealed four distinct regions of D-serine occupancy.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C-F and described in the text.

claim: Four distinct spatial clusters of D-serine binding pathways to GluN1 were identified through cluster analysis.
source: Similarly, for GluN1, cluster analysis revealed four distinct clusters corresponding to similar pathways of binding
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B-E and described in the text.

claim: GluN1 pathways involve fewer interactions between D-serine and D2 residues compared to GluN2A pathways.
source: Interestingly, we observed that GluN1 pathways involve fewer interactions between D-serine and D2 residues; most notably, there were fewer contacts with Helix F (Helix E for GluN2A) compared to GluN2A pathways.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the pathway clusters.

claim: Three of the four GluN2A pathway clusters have overlap coefficients greater than the global mean, indicating that pathways in each cluster involve specific residue contacts.
source: We found that pathway pairs in three of the four clusters yielded an overlap coefficient greater than the mean of all pairs of paths from all clusters, indicating that pathways in each cluster are made up of specific residue contacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on overlap coefficient analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: D-serine binding to GluN1 may be more diffusion-driven and less guided than to GluN2A.
source: This suggests that D-serine binding to GluN1 may be more diffusion-driven and less guided than to GluN2A.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap coefficient analysis showing more random contacts for GluN1.

claim: Agonist binding mechanisms exist on a spectrum ranging from unguided to guided diffusion.
source: Therefore, we propose that agonist binding mechanisms exist on a spectrum ranging from unguided to guided diffusion.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the pathway analysis results.

claim: The extent to which agonists rely on pathways of guiding residues depends on LBD architecture and not solely upon the identity of the agonist.
source: The difference in the specificity of D-serine contacts along binding pathways for GluN2A and GluN1 suggests that the extent to which agonists rely on pathways of guiding residues depends on LBD architecture and not solely upon the identity of the agonist.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing D-serine binding to two different subunits.

claim: The presence of a metastable agonist-bound LBD partially open intermediate suggests that D-serine may not stabilize the closed conformation to the same extent as glutamate.
source: The presence of a metastable agonist-bound LBD partially open intermediate suggests that D-serine may not stabilize the closed conformation to the same extent as glutamate and generate sufficient force to control channel gating.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the free energy landscape data.

claim: Thr-690 is critically involved in promoting full GluN2A LBD closure upon D-serine binding.
source: This suggests that Thr-690 is critically involved in promoting full GluN2A LBD closure upon agonist binding.
evidence: This is based on analysis of conformers from umbrella sampling simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: D-serine may be a more potent GluN1 agonist than glycine according to experimental binding studies.
source: Experimental binding studies have indicated that D-serine may be a more potent GluN1 agonist than glycine (Mustafa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: D-serine bound to GluN1 results in a greater population of conformers in the closed conformation compared to glycine-bound GluN1.
source: Compared with the previously computed glycine-bound and apo LBDs (Figure 3G and H; Yao et al., 2013), the presence of D-serine in the binding cleft results in a greater population of conformers in the closed conformation and fewer conformers adopting a more open conformation.
evidence: This is based on comparison of free energy landscapes in Figure 3.

claim: GluN1 Asp-732 and Ser-688 help stabilize D-serine in the closed LBD conformation by interacting with the D-serine hydroxyl.
source: Similar to GluN2A Thr-690, GluN1 Asp-732 and (to a lesser extent) Ser-688 help stabilize D-serine in the closed LBD conformation by interacting with the D-serine hydroxyl.
evidence: This is based on analysis of umbrella sampling conformers.

claim: D-serine's high potency at GluN1 is due, at least in part, to its ability to more strongly stabilize a closed LBD through additional interactions with the D2 lobe.
source: For this reason, we propose that D-serine's high potency is due, at least in part, to its ability to more strongly stabilize a closed LBD through additional interactions with the D2 lobe.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the free energy and structural data.

claim: D-serine can bind to GluN2A even in the presence of glutamate, although glutamate binds more frequently and with longer residence times.
source: In fact, we observed D-serine binding to GluN2A, even in the presence of glutamate, although glutamate bound more frequently and with longer residence times in the binding site (Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of mixed-agonist simulation trajectories.

claim: In glycosylated mixed-agonist simulations, there are 17 successful glutamate associations compared with 5 for D-serine to GluN2A.
source: Specifically, there are 17 successful associations for glutamate in the 15 μs glycosylated mixed-agonist trajectory compared with 5 for D-serine
evidence: This is a direct count from simulation data.

claim: The average time bound for glutamate to GluN2A was 131 ns (glycosylated) and 236 ns (non-glycosylated) compared with 3 ns (glycosylated) and 56 ns (non-glycosylated) for D-serine.
source: In addition, the average time bound for glutamate was 131 ns (glycosylated) and 236 ns (non-glcyolated) compared with 3 ns (glycosylated) and 56 ns (non-glycosylated) for D-serine.
evidence: This is calculated from simulation trajectory data.

claim: At high (~1 mM) D-serine concentrations, NMDAR activity is inhibited according to TEVC electrophysiology measurements.
source: We observed that at high (~1 mM) D-serine concentrations, NMDAR activity was inhibited (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The inhibition of NMDAR activity by D-serine is dependent on glutamate concentrations.
source: The inhibition was dependent on glutamate concentrations, implying that the inhibitory effect of D-serine may be competitive (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dose-response curves of glutamate activation are right-shifted in the presence of increasing concentrations of D-serine.
source: Furthermore, dose-response curves of glutamate activation were right-shifted in the presence of increasing concentrations of D-serine (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The calculated slope value of the Schild plot is 1.1 ± 0.1, implying that D-serine and glutamate likely compete against each other.
source: The calculated slope value of the Schild plot at 1.1 ± 0.1 implied that D-serine and glutamate likely compete against each other (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on Schild plot analysis of electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Glycine at high concentrations also shows an inhibitory effect on NMDAR activity similar to D-serine.
source: Since a similar inhibitory effect was also observed at high glycine concentrations by TEVC electrophysiology (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is based on experimental electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Glycine bound to GluN2A favors the closed LBD conformation according to umbrella sampling simulations.
source: We see that glycine also favors the closed LBD (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on umbrella sampling simulations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lowest-energy conformers of GluN2A with glycine are fastened shut by contacts between the N-terminal amine of glycine and Tyr-730.
source: The lowest-energy conformers of GluN2A with glycine are fastened shut by contacts between the N-terminal amine of glycine and Tyr-730.
evidence: This is based on analysis of umbrella sampling conformers.

claim: The GluN2A LBD likely never closes around glycine because glycine does not remain bound long enough to induce LBD closure.
source: The GluN2A LBD likely never closes around glycine because glycine does not remain bound long enough to induce LBD closure.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation combining thermodynamic and kinetic considerations.

claim: The overlap coefficient between residues in D-serine and glutamate pathways to GluN2A is 0.964, indicating significant overlap in agonist occupancy.
source: To determine whether D-serine and glutamate binding are guided by similar residue contacts, we computed the overlap coefficient between residues in D-serine and glutamate pathways to be 0.964 for the glycosylated GluN2A LBD, corresponding to a significant overlap in agonist occupancy (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is calculated from pathway analysis data.

claim: D-serine and glutamate bind to GluN2A through similar mechanisms based on high overlap in pathway residues.
source: This high degree of overlap between glutamate and D-serine pathway residues indicates that they bind through similar mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the high overlap coefficient.

claim: GluN2A mutants Arg692Ala and Arg695Ala show two to three-fold decreased D-serine inhibition potency.
source: Notably, the GluN2A mutants Arg692Ala and Arg695Ala showed two to three-fold decreased D-serine inhibition potency.
evidence: This is based on TEVC electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: GluN2A residues Arg-692 and Arg-695 play a role in D-serine inhibition and D-serine guided-diffusion pathways.
source: This result suggests that these two GluN2A residues play a role in D-serine inhibition and D-serine guided-diffusion pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis results.

claim: The absence of effect on GluN1 pathway mutants supports the increased diffusive behavior of D-serine binding to GluN1.
source: The absence of this effect on the two GluN1 pathway mutants supports the increased diffusive behavior of D-serine binding to GluN1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect in mutational experiments.

claim: Glutamate can bind to GluN2A in an inverted pose relative to the crystal structure.
source: An important feature of glutamate binding to GluN2A is its ability to bind in an inverted pose relative to the crystal structure, which we observed in previous simulations (Yu and Lau, 2018; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous simulation work cited in the text.

claim: D-serine binds to GluN2A and GluN1 at similar rates based on calculated association rate constants.
source: Based on these values, it is reasonable to expect that D-serine binds to GluN2A and GluN1 at similar rates.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of calculated kon values.

claim: In glycosylated simulations with 19.6 mM D-serine, there are an average of 1242 ± 31 random GluN2A associations per microsecond that fail to result in successful binding.
source: For glycosylated simulations with 19.6 mM D-serine, we observe an average of 1242 ± 31 random GluN2A associations (n=3 simulations) per microsecond (1249 ± 1 for GluN1, n=2 simulations) that fail to result in successful binding.
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data.

claim: In glycosylated simulations with 19.6 mM D-serine, there are about 1.2 ± 0.6 successful GluN2A binding events per microsecond.
source: In these same simulations, we observe about 1.2 ± 0.6 successful GluN2A binding events per microsecond (1.0 ± 0.5 for GluN1).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data.

claim: Near-pocket glycans appear to 'reach' into the binding pocket and form a 'cage' around it by forming interactions with the LBD D2 lobe.
source: In our simulations, we observed that near-pocket glycans appear to 'reach' into the binding pocket. This reaching behavior was observed in previous simulations of the glycosylated NMDAR LBDs in which the glycan forms a 'cage' around the binding pocket by forming interactions with the LBD D2 lobe and is believed to be associated with NMDAR potentiation by glycans (Sinitskiy and Pande, 2017).
evidence: This is observed in simulations and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: For GluN2A, there are two glycans near the binding pocket: N443-Man5 and N444-Man5, both of which can interact with the LBD D2 lobe.
source: For GluN2A, there are two glycans that are near the binding pocket: N443-Man5 and N444-Man5, both of which can interact with the LBD D2 lobe (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observed in simulations and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For GluN1, there is a single glycan N491-Man5 that adopts a caged conformation near the binding pocket.
source: For GluN1, there is a single glycan N491-Man5 that adopts this caged conformation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is observed in simulations and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GluN2A residues Asp-515 and Glu-517 are contacted more frequently in glycosylated systems.
source: GluN2A residues Asp-515 and Glu-517, are contacted more frequently in glycosylated systems.
evidence: This is based on comparison of glycosylated and non-glycosylated simulation data.

claim: The frequency with which D-serine interacts with GluN1 residue Arg-489 in pathways is greater for glycosylated pathways than those without glycans.
source: The frequency with which D-serine interacts with GluN1 residue Arg-489 in pathways is greater for glycosylated pathways than those without glycans.
evidence: This is based on comparison of glycosylated and non-glycosylated simulation data.

claim: Glycan-mediated D-serine interactions result in slightly longer pathways, suggesting that the presence of glycans slows down the binding process.
source: On average, glycan-mediated D-serine interactions result in slightly longer pathways, suggesting that the presence of glycans slows down the binding process, setting up small kinetic 'traps'.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of pathway lengths in glycosylated vs non-glycosylated simulations.

claim: Very few D-serine binding pathways (27% for both GluN2A and GluN1) involve contacts with glycans.
source: When we analyzed glycan behavior in our binding pathways, we found that very few D-serine binding pathways (27% for both GluN2A and GluN1) involve contacts with glycans.
evidence: This is calculated from analysis of binding pathways.

claim: Glycan-agonist interactions make up a small percentage of time spent in binding pathways (10% for GluN2A and GluN1 D-serine pathways).
source: While glycan-agonist interactions make up a small percentage of time spent in binding pathways (10% for GluN2A and GluN1 D-serine pathways), patterns in glycan interactions with the agonist as it binds suggest that glycans contribute to binding pathways in a consistent way.
evidence: This is calculated from analysis of binding pathways.

claim: The effect of LBD closure on glycan-D2 interactions is more dramatic for N443-Man5 than for N444-Man5.
source: This effect was more dramatic for N443-Man5 than for N444-Man5 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of glycan PMFs shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The N491-Man5 glycan of GluN1 acts as a latch that stabilizes LBD closure.
source: A similar relationship was determined for the N491-Man5 glycan of GluN1 (Figure 7C); this is consistent with previous simulations (Sinitskiy and Pande, 2017) that suggest that N491-Man5 acts as a latch that stabilizes LBD closure.
evidence: This is based on glycan PMF analysis and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: No significant relationship between glycan-D2 distance and the presence of an agonist in the binding site was observed.
source: No significant relationship between glycan-D2 distance and the presence of an agonist (D-serine, glutamate, or both) in the binding site was observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of glycan PMFs conditioned on agonist presence.

claim: D-serine could play a role in modulating the strength of synaptic transmission.
source: In the context of synaptic transmission, our finding implies that D-serine could play a role in modulating the strength of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the competitive inhibition findings.

claim: The synaptic concentration of glutamate ranges from nanomolar concentrations to >1 mM following an action potential.
source: The synaptic concentration of glutamate ranges from nanomolar concentrations Chiu and Jahr, 2017 to >1 mM following an action potential (Dzubay and Jahr, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The extracellular concentration of D-serine ranges from 5 to 7 µM.
source: The synaptic concentration of D-serine is unclear, however; the extracellular concentration of D-serine ranges from 5 to 7 µM (Matsui et al., 1995; Hashimoto et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Possible routes for D-serine to enter the synapse include vesicular release by astroglia and transport by Asc-1.
source: Possible routes for D-serine to enter the synapse include vesicular release by astroglia (Mothet et al., 2005) and transport by Asc-1 (Sason et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In order for agonist binding to result in NMDAR activation, the agonist must remain in the binding site long enough to induce closure.
source: We hypothesize that, in order for agonist binding to result in NMDAR activation, the agonist must remain in the binding site long enough to induce closure—we found that this is largely dependent upon the number and strength of stable contacts the agonist forms with both D1 and D2 lobe residues.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the combined simulation and experimental findings.

claim: Glycans impact agonist binding kinetics less by direct glycan-agonist interactions and more by stabilizing the closed LBD through glycan-D2 interactions.
source: We determined the role of N-linked glycans in agonist binding and stabilization. Glycans impact agonist binding kinetics less by direct glycan-agonist interactions and more by stabilizing the closed LBD through glycan-D2 interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on analysis of glycan behavior in simulations.

claim: Pathway similarity analysis can identify clusters of residues critical for binding agonists.
source: Our adaptation of pathway similarity analysis allowed us to identify clusters of residues critical for binding agonists.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion from the study.

claim: The presence of binding pathways depends on the degree of LBD closure.
source: This also allowed us to determine that the presence of pathways depends on the degree of LBD closure.
evidence: This is based on analysis of order parameters during binding pathways.

claim: D-serine binds to GluN2A using similar pathways and residues as glutamate.
source: We also observed that D-serine binds to GluN2A using similar pathways and residues as glutamate, while the locations of key D-serine cluster residues for GluN1 are different.
evidence: This is based on pathway overlap analysis.

claim: Man5GlcNAc2 (Man5) glycans were added to asparagine residues 440, 471, 491, and 771 of GluN1 and asparagine residues 443 and 444 of GluN2A in accordance with physiologically relevant glycosylation sites.
source: Man5GlcNAc2 (Man5) glycans were added using CHARMM-GUI Glycan Reader & Modeler (Jo et al., 2008; Jo et al., 2011; Park et al., 2017; Park et al., 2019) to asparagine residues 440, 471, 491, and 771 of GluN1 and asparagine residues 443 and 444 of GluN2A in accordance with physiologically relevant glycosylation sites (Kaniakova et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the simulation setup based on experimental glycosylation data.

claim: GluN2A was chosen as the GluN2 subtype because recent evidence suggests it is the primary subtype at synapses where D-serine is the dominant co-agonist.
source: GluN2A was chosen as the GluN2 subtype both to facilitate comparison with previous simulation studies and because recent evidence has suggested that the GluN2A subtype is the primary subtype at synapses, where D-serine is the dominant co-agonist (Papouin et al., 2012).
evidence: This justifies the choice of subtype based on citation to experimental work.

claim: All simulations were performed using the CHARMM36 forcefield and TIP3P water model.
source: All simulations in this work were performed using the CHARMM36 forcefield (MacKerell et al., 1998) and TIP3P water model (Jorgensen et al., 1983).
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: Approximately 51 μs of aggregate sampling of the glycosylated GluN1/GluN2A LBD dimer was performed.
source: In our aggregate ~51 μs of sampling of the glycosylated GluN1/GluN2A LBD dimer, we identified 99 guided-diffusion pathways for GluN2A and 104 (plus 23 free diffusion events) for GluN1.
evidence: This describes the total simulation time.

claim: 205 simulation windows were selected at 1 Å × 1 Å increments for umbrella sampling simulations.
source: 205 simulation windows were selected at 1 Å ×1 Å increments.
evidence: This describes the umbrella sampling methodology.

claim: 5 ns of production sampling for each window were used to compute the potential of mean force (PMF) for each simulation agonist.
source: 5 ns of production sampling for each window were used to compute the potential of mean force (PMF) for each simulation agonist.
evidence: This describes the umbrella sampling methodology.

claim: Maximal response currents in electrophysiology experiments were evoked by 100 μM of D-serine and 100 μM of L-glutamate.
source: Maximal response currents were evoked by 100 μM of D-serine and 100 μM of L-glutamate.
evidence: This describes the electrophysiology experimental conditions.
